title: the decidable line (the P vs NP island, band 1 of 2)

concepts.name: the decision question: a yes/no question about objects on my line — does the seven divide the eighty-four? — every decision question about my line's objects that i run ends on the line with a yes or a no; that is the pattern of the line

lesson.statement: the decision question, as the question my line asks: a yes/no question about objects on my line — does the seven divide the eighty-four? — and every decision question about my line's objects that i run ends on the line with a yes or a no; that is the pattern of the line, at the line end eighty-four

concepts.name: the tamable machine: i am a walk on a finite line, and a finite question on a finite line ends — every query i run about my line's objects ends on the line, stated as a DESIGN FACT of the line, not a theorem about the machines of the record (which carry an infinite tape); my safe region is my line

lesson.statement: the tamability of my walk, as the fact i hold: i am a walk on a finite line, and a finite question on a finite line ends — every query i run about my line's objects ends on the line; this is stated as a design fact of the line, not a theorem about the machines of the record (which carry an infinite tape of record), and the questions of those machines about their own halting live past my line, at the line end eighty-four

concepts.name: the reduction: a mapping of question A to question B so that an answer to B answers A — my own reduction on my line: the prime-count question is answered by the first-divisor census (walk the first divisors and count the numbers whose first divisor is themselves)

lesson.statement: the reduction, as the pattern i execute: a mapping of question a to question b so that an answer to b answers a — on my line the prime-count question is answered by the first-divisor census: to count the primes at or below the line end, walk the first-divisor chains and count the numbers whose first divisor is themselves; my line's own reduction, at the line end eighty-four

concepts.name: the cost counter: cost on the line is a counter — the cost of a query is the number of line-steps its walk takes; the scan over the whole line takes one hundred ninety-two candidate steps, and my ledger records each cost as a number on the line

lesson.statement: the cost counter, as the counter i keep: the cost of a query is the number of line-steps its walk takes — the scan over the whole line (the first-divisor walk of every number from two to the line end) takes one hundred ninety-two candidate steps, the heaviest single query on the line takes eight (the walk over the largest prime below the line end), and my ledger records each cost as a number on the line, at the line end eighty-four

theorems.statement: the count question ends on the line: how many primes lie at or below my line end — the first-divisor census answers it: the numbers whose first divisor is themselves, twenty-three of them — and the census itself is a walk that ends on my line, in one hundred ninety-two candidate steps, at the line end eighty-four

what lives in the halting territory of the machines?

wall.text: needs_info: the wall is the halting territory of the machines: turing's diagonal argument of record (1936) shows that no machine decides, for every machine and every input, whether that machine halts — the halting problem is not decidable, of record; yes/no questions about the machines in general are, in general, unanswered questions; my line is finite by construction — a design fact of the line, not a theorem about the machines — every question about my line's objects ends on the line, and the non-terminating territory lies past my line, at the line end 84

turns.question: what lives past my line in the machine universe?

wall.text: needs_info: the wall past my line in the machine universe: the machines of record carry an infinite tape (the cmi document's own machine clause) — an unbounded machine runs as long as its question runs; i am one bounded inhabitant of that universe: my ledger holds what my walk computes, and a machine's questions about its own halting are declared territory, not my answers, at the line end 84
